doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

chapter: Power of music and big-band life
title: Blue notes, Western theory and balance
summary: MR raises blue notes; Jimmy argues the Western system divides music up and talks of vibration and balance across cultures.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Well that’s what — among the things I love about the blues is that you can play the quote wrong notes, the blue notes, that clash theoretically, but that they still sound so good.
Yeah. They never go straight on.

And the other reason is because of dealing with the system in terms of the western world, we scientifically divided everything up. There’s nothing wrong with that. But to make that the total aspect of what music is about, is where the negative aspect of conveying that message you see. When it came to opera, I mean [inaudible] — they didn’t know anything about China. And anything that sounded strange, they would say it’s Chinese music. But they’re in deep trouble now you see. Globally, they’re in deep trouble. All of a sudden they find out there’s other people living elsewhere. And they have their respective cultures according to the creative process that we live in.
And how does that fit in? How are we going to resolve that with our own eight note scale?

Well the whole thing is we’re coming, see we come to grips with that because, again, when we speak in terms of poverty, at least from my point of view I like to look at the aspect of creation. You’re dealing with such a fine sense, I say we are vibration — balance. And so we can go to China and say, or Japan and say yin yang, or wherever it is, they’ve got a word for balance you see. And music speaks strongly to the nature of what we all are about in terms of the creative process. And we have a choice how we wish to use it in terms of our given talents.
